agent_notes: The superscription is verse 1 in the Hebrew and verse 0 in the KJV, so every later verse here is one number higher than the KJV's. I translated it as a heading and kept 'alamoth' as a transliteration. The meaning of 'alamoth' is uncertain: 'maidens', 'high voices' or an instrument. The packet's Rashi and Meiri both take it as an instrument, citing 1 Chr 15:20.

Literal layer keeps 'carts' (agalot). Rashi and Malbim read war chariots and Metzudat David wagons made for war; the commentary and note now present 'chariot' as a supported interpretation, not an error. I removed my earlier claim about changing verb tenses, which the forms do not support (imperfect, weqatal, imperfect). The Targum reading 'round shields' is taken from the packet's Aramaic text (עֲגִילִין) and is my own reading of it.

agent_notes: הַרְפּוּ is plural and addressed to the nations (Rashi, Radak, Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David all agree). The popular reading 'be still' as personal calm is a later reuse; I kept 'let go' in the literal layer and the nations' context in the commentary, since the KJV 'Be still' hides the military sense.
Literal layer now 'a high refuge', exactly as in verse 8. I also removed the claim that the refrain is 'left out after verse 4'; I describe only what the text has.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses בְּהָמִיר as 'when changes' and lists the lemma as מוּר (hiphil infinitive). I read it as 'when the earth changes places', from מוּר 'to exchange'. The KJV 'be removed' is a fair guess; YLT and ASV render 'changing / change'. Rashi's Isaiah 51:6 parallel is his end-of-days reading of the psalm, not a lexical point; I cite him only for Metzudat Zion's link with תמורה.

agent_notes: לִפְנוֹת בֹּקֶר is literally 'at the turning of morning'. The KJV 'right early' and BBE 'at the dawn' are interpretations. Ibn Ezra reads 'the time close to day, or every day'; Meiri compares 'when the day turns' (Jer 6:4). I kept 'at the turning of morning' in the literal layer and 'when morning turns' in the dramatic one.
